generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, referencing is how you credit the sources your work builds on. When you draw on an idea, a finding or an argument from your reading, a reference records whose it was and where it was published. A reader can then tell your own thinking from the work you are drawing on, and trace it back to its source. Crediting that work is part of academic integrity, and the reference list also shows a marker the range of reading behind your writing.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students using the same book chapter in an essay.

{{learner-a}} uses the chapter's idea and, at the end, adds it to a reference list so as not to be accused of copying. The source is listed, but {{learner-a}} treats referencing only as a way of staying out of trouble, added once the writing is done. Whether the idea is clearly credited where it is used, or whether the list shows the reading behind the work, has not really been considered. This treats referencing as a chore.

{{learner-b}} references the same chapter as the idea is used, naming the author in the text and giving the full details in the list. For {{learner-b}}, the reference credits the author whose idea this is, keeps the line between borrowed and original thinking clear, and shows a marker the reading behind the argument. Avoiding plagiarism follows from this, rather than being the whole point.

Both students listed the source. Only {{learner-b}} used referencing for what it is really for: crediting ideas and evidencing reading.
generatedProse.summary: Referencing is how you acknowledge where the knowledge in your work comes from, not a chore bolted on at the end. You can now explain what referencing is and say why it matters: it credits the people whose ideas you use, it is part of academic integrity, and it shows a tutor the scope of your reading. The next lessons turn this purpose into practice - the styles and parts of a reference, and how to reference accurately when you quote and paraphrase.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s use of the reference go beyond avoiding plagiarism?

items.text: Crediting the author's idea and showing the reading behind the argument.
Listing the source once the essay was finished.
Leaving out quotation marks so the writing looked original.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} referenced to credit the author and evidence the reading, not just to avoid plagiarism.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what the reference did beyond keeping {{learner-b}} out of trouble.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} used the reference to credit the author's idea and show the reading behind the work. Listing late, piling up sources or hiding a borrowing are not the point.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
